chapter.title: Ticket Closed
chapter.sub: Nine tickets. Nine “Resolved.” One problem nobody owned.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the season map ahead of its production-bible entry · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 3 · EPISODE 8 · DRAFT  Cold case · Sam · Level L3 (Technician) · CASE-016  Sam has closed the same ticket nine times. At eleven at night he writes a resignation letter — and finally looks at a photo he took that morning.  ⚑ RV-74 · RV-76 · Q-014: service-management practice simplified; Sam's wellbeing is handled with care; CASE-016 is a proposed SIGNAL original. Some choices in this episode run on a clock.

items.title: Nine Times
items.stakes: Sam has closed the same ticket nine times since spring. Last night he wrote a resignation letter. It's still in drafts.
items.clock: 7:52 a.m. — seven and a half minutes to a client call.
items.reward: The first problem Sam has ever owned. The ghost, finally caught.

objectives.text: Find who switches the room at 7:00
Don't pull the plug on the ghost box — yet
Look closer: two things older than anyone's badge

items.rumor: The server that switches the Garden Room every morning was decommissioned two years ago. It didn't get the memo.

items.alt: The Garden Room. The wall display shows a blue box: NO SIGNAL, HDMI 2. A salesperson, arms up, stands by the table; the touch panel reads HDMI 2.

bubbles.text: Client call at eight. It says No Signal. Again. Is this room cursed?

items.caption: The ninth time since spring. Sam knows the fix by heart.

items.alt: Sam arrives at a jog, phone in hand, heading for the touch panel.

bubbles.text: Morning. I know this one. Give me ten seconds.

items.caption: He says “I know this one” a lot. It's true every time.

items.prompt: 7:52:30. Seven and a half minutes to the client call. The display is on HDMI 2. What does Sam do?
items.happening: The display is on the wrong input — again.
items.risk: A client call, and a salesperson's trust in the room.
timeout: The salesperson unplugs everything and plugs it back in. The display sits on HDMI 2 until 8:03.
When you know the fix, not deciding is the only way to fail.

hints.text: Restore it — without destroying anything you might need later.

options.label: Reboot the display — clean start
options.result: Ninety seconds of black. It boots on HDMI 1. Its input history resets with it.
options.consequence: Works this morning. Tomorrow at seven it happens again — and now nobody can see why.
options.fail: You erased the one record that names what switched it.

options.label: Snap a photo of the display's info screen, then switch to HDMI 1 from the panel
options.result: Ten seconds: a photo out of habit, one tap, HDMI 1. The proposal slide appears.
options.consequence: The meeting starts on time. The photo sits in his camera roll.

options.label: Swap the HDMI cable
options.result: Two minutes under the table. New cable, still HDMI 2 selected.
options.consequence: The cable was never the problem.
options.fail: Changing parts before reading the state.

options.label: Move the call to another room
options.result: They pack up and walk. The other room is booked at 8:30.
options.consequence: It works, and it moves the problem instead of solving the morning.

items.alt: The Garden Room at 7:59: the proposal is on the display on HDMI 1. The sales lead, relieved, gestures at it; Sam, by the door, gives a small wave.

bubbles.text: You're a lifesaver. Same time next week?
…Probably.

items.caption: She meant it as a joke. He heard it as a schedule.

lines.text: You're a lifesaver. Same time next week?

items.alt: The photo on Sam's phone: the display's info screen. Input HDMI 2. Last change 07:00:00. Source: control, network. Uptime 412 days.
items.caption: He took the photo out of habit. He won't look at it until eleven tonight.

items.alt: Back at the service desk, Sam's screen: ticket 5120, Garden Room, display on wrong input, switched to HDMI 1, resolved in 41 seconds. Below: similar tickets, 8.
items.caption: Forty-one seconds. His fastest yet. It doesn't feel like winning.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #29 · AVERY'S LENS  Fix the pattern, not the instance  When the same pain repeats, the interface or system is telling you something.  Nine tickets, one 07:00 ghost. Closing each ticket fixed nothing for the person in the room.

items.alt: Sam's kitchen at night, lit by a laptop. On the screen, a draft letter: Dear Imani, I've decided to move on. I'm grateful for — and the cursor blinks.
narration: He'd written three drafts. This one was the kind one.

items.alt: Sam's closed tickets for the Garden Room, listed by date: every one opened between 07:02 and 07:55, every one fixed the same way, the last one today.
items.caption: Every one before eight. Every one on a weekday. He'd never seen them on one screen.

items.title: All before 8 a.m. All weekdays.
items.body: He'd never seen them together. Nobody had. Each one was fast and correct and completely useless. Together they are a clock.

items.alt: Sam, arms up in surprise, holds up his phone: the zoomed photo reads last change 07:00:00, source CONTROL.

bubbles.text: Source: control. Not a person. Seven o'clock exactly. Every time I got there, it had already happened.

items.title: Nobody touched it
items.body: Sam's closure notes blamed early risers plugging laptops into HDMI 2. The display's own log says the input changed at 07:00:00 on the dot, by a network control command — before anyone was in the room. Look back: every ticket opened between 07:02 and 07:55, weekdays only, and the photo he took at 7:52 said so.
items.label: Test: the Clue Board. Which three clues separate the explanations?

items.alt: Split scene: Sam at his kitchen table on the phone; Priya, also still up, answers from somewhere with the same dim light.

bubbles.text: Sorry, it's late. I think a machine is switching the Garden Room every morning at seven. And I've closed it nine times.
Then it's not your ninth incident. It's your first problem. Go to sleep. Meet me at 6:45 — bring the photo.

items.prompt: (11:48 p.m., a message.) Sam? Why are you awake. Why are you sending me a spreadsheet.

options.label: (As Sam) “I think a machine switches the Garden Room at seven. I've closed it nine times.”
options.reply: Then it's not your ninth incident. It's your first problem. Sleep. 6:45.

options.label: (As Sam) “Sorry. Ignore it. It's nothing.”
options.reply: It's midnight and it's a spreadsheet. It's not nothing.

options.label: (As Sam) “I'm quitting.”
options.reply: Not at midnight you're not. 6:45. Bring the photo.

items.alt: In the empty early-morning office, Priya has written three words on a whiteboard: incident — restore it, fast; problem — remove the cause; change — do it safely, on the record.

bubbles.text: You've done incident work perfectly. Nine times. Nobody ever handed you the problem to own.
So I'm not bad at my job.

items.caption: “You're bad at a job nobody gave you,” Priya says. “That's different.”

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Sam and Maya beside a board. An incident gets the room working. A problem record chases the root cause, so it stops happening. How do I justify a real fix? Payback: hours invested over hours saved a week. Eight hours of work that saves two hours a week pays back in four weeks.

bubbles.text: An incident gets the room working. A problem record chases the root cause, so it stops happening.
How do I justify a real fix?
Payback: hours invested over hours saved a week. Eight hours of work that saves two hours a week pays back in four weeks.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    Problem record   A tracked item for the underlying cause behind repeated incidents, with an owner and a fix.   Root cause   The underlying reason a fault happened, as opposed to the symptom people noticed.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Payback time  weeks = hours invested ÷ hours saved per week   hours invested  one-off effort  hours saved per week  recurring cost removed    Worked example.  8 hours of work that saves 2 hours a week: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 weeks to pay back.

📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 29 OF 31 · PP. 172–173, 177–180  PART 11 OPERATIONS  Page 178:  If it's not documented, it doesn't exist.  Ray's handwriting from years ago. Maya added the date and signed underneath.

items.label: **Fieldbook module 29 — Operations — roles, hand-offs and “write it down”.** Beginner support: every new word is defined, and every formula comes with its variables and a worked example.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · module 29 · tap a plate to open it full size     Operations create consistency     Roles and handoffs     Operational philosophy     Teams thrive when leadership prepares

items.label: **Learn it now:** incident, problem and change — and why nine fast fixes can still be a failure.

items.prompt: 6:47. If the pattern holds, the display switches at 7:00. How do you catch it?
items.happening: The fault arrives on a schedule. Thirteen minutes to set up.
known: ▮ Display log: change at 07:00:00, source CONTROL
timeout: At 7:00:00 the display switches while you're still arguing about how to watch it.
A scheduled fault gives you one chance a day. Plan before it arrives.

hints.text: Catch it without changing anything first.

options.label: Reboot the display now so it starts clean
options.result: It reboots. Its history of 7:00 changes is gone. At 7:00 it switches anyway — with nothing to compare.
options.consequence: A clean start erased the pattern.
options.fail: You destroyed the evidence right before the event you came to watch.

options.label: Unplug the display's network cable so nothing can switch it
options.result: 7:00 comes and goes. Nothing happens — including the answer.
options.consequence: The room's panel can't reach the display now, either.
options.fail: Preventing the symptom also prevented the diagnosis — and broke the room's control.

options.label: Priya captures at the display's switch port — hers — while Sam watches the display's log
options.result: Two views of one moment: what arrived on the wire, what the display did.
options.consequence: Evidence two people can sign, gathered by the network's owner.

options.label: Sam plugs his laptop into the room's wall port and captures traffic himself
options.result: Mei's alert fires before the laptop finishes booting: unknown device on the building network.
options.consequence: Not his network, not an approved device.
options.fail: Measuring someone else's network without them is a boundary, not a shortcut.

items.alt: The Garden Room at exactly 7:00:00. The display flips to NO SIGNAL, HDMI 2. Sam's arms go up. Priya's laptop shows her capture from switch port 3-14: at 07:00:00.004, a command from address .47, input 2.
items.caption: Nobody in the room. The display moved anyway.

items.alt: Inventory entry for address .47: Room scheduler, legacy. Location: riser closet 3B. Status: decommissioned, two years ago. Sam and Priya look up from it.
items.caption: Decommissioned two years ago. It just switched a display eleven seconds ago.

lines.text: It switched. Nobody's in the room. It just— it switched.

items.title: The server that doesn't exist
items.body: The command didn't come from the room's controller or from a person. It came from a legacy scheduler the inventory swears was decommissioned two years ago. Someone wrote “decommissioned” as a plan; nobody checked that the box went dark. It has been running an old configuration's 7:00 wake job ever since — and the Garden Room's display kept the old address it was aimed at.
items.label: Test: reason from a record that lies. What does it tell you, and what must you know before anyone touches the box?

items.alt: System View of the 7:00 command's path. A legacy scheduler in riser closet 3B, powered, listed in the inventory as decommissioned, sends a 7:00 job over the building control network, owned by Priya, to twelve targets: the Garden Room display (input to HDMI 2), a lobby sign on a reused address (input switched, unnoticed), a projector in a room that no longer exists (still answers), and nine addresses that don't reply.
items.caption: Twelve targets. One owner-less box. Nine “Resolved” tickets.

items.title: Ask why five times
items.body: Taiichi Ohno, the engineer who shaped a Japanese carmaker's production system from the 1950s on, taught teams to ask “why?” about five times when something failed — past the first answer, which is usually a symptom. His 1978 book walks through a machine that stopped: a blown fuse, from an overload, from poor lubrication, from a worn pump, from a missing strainer that let metal scrap in. Five is a habit, not a rule. The point is to keep asking until the fix stops the whole chain.

items.alt: The ground-floor lobby. The welcome sign shows its own loop — on input 2, since 7:00. The receptionist, amused, talks to Priya, who is writing.

bubbles.text: The sign? It blinks every morning at seven. I thought it was saying good morning.
It's being told good morning. By a box that doesn't exist.

items.caption: Target two of twelve. Nobody ever filed a ticket: the sign's input 2 happens to be its welcome loop.

items.alt: Riser closet 3B: racks, a patch panel, and on a shelf a gray box labeled ROOM SCHEDULER (legacy), its lights on. A hand-written sticker under it: DECOMMISSIONED? A Facilities technician stands at the door; Sam points at the box.

bubbles.text: That box? Older than my badge. We were told never to touch it.
It's been switching my room every morning for two years.

items.caption: The box was never turned off. It was only written off.

items.title: A label, handwritten
items.body: *DO NOT TOUCH — scheduling (R.)* The facilities tech has worked here nine years and was told never to touch it. Nobody remembers who told him. The R. is in a familiar font.

items.prompt: The ghost box is in front of Sam, lights on. What now?
items.happening: Cause found: an unowned box, still running. Its power cable is right there.
items.risk: Twelve addresses' worth of things nobody has mapped.
timeout: The Facilities tech, tired of waiting, says “just unplug it then” and does.
An idle expert hands the decision to the nearest person with a hand free.

hints.text: Whose box, whose network, whose closet?

options.label: Pull its power cable — problem solved
options.result: The Garden Room stops switching. So does something in the lobby, and a building alarm panel that polled the box logs a fault Facilities spends two days chasing.
options.consequence: You found the other dependents by breaking them.
options.fail: Not your equipment, unmapped, and no change. Finding the cause doesn't authorize removing it.

options.label: Log in with the default password on its sticker to disable the job
options.result: Mei's phone buzzes within a minute: a default credential used on an unmanaged device.
options.consequence: Now it's a security incident, and you're in the middle of it.
options.fail: Access decisions belong to Mei. A default password isn't permission.

options.label: Map everything it commands, find its owner, and raise a change with Priya and Facilities to disable only the 7:00 job
options.result: Priya lists twelve targets; three still answer. Facilities takes ownership. The change has a rollback and a 7:00 test.

options.label: Block its traffic on the switch yourself
options.result: You don't have access to the switch. If you did, it would be Priya's network you just changed.
options.fail: The network belongs to Priya. Changes to it go through her.

items.alt: Back at the desks, Sam speaks quietly; Priya listens.

bubbles.text: Last night I wrote a resignation letter. It's still in drafts.
Keep it there. Present this first. Then decide — with the whole picture, not at eleven at night.

items.caption: She didn't tell him not to. She told him not yet.

lines.text: Last night I wrote a resignation letter.
Keep it there. Present this first. Then decide — with the whole picture, not at eleven at night.

items.label: **Service Mode:** 6:57 a.m. The fault arrives at 7:00. Be ready for it.
**Sequence:** from nine incidents to one problem.

items.alt: Monday's change board on a monitor: change CHG-3302 approved — disable only the 7:00 job; owners Facilities and Priya; rollback re-enable; test Tuesday at 7:00 on three devices; then decommission properly. Mei, who sits on the board, holds the printed record.

bubbles.text: First change I've approved this month that came with a map of everything it touches. Who wrote it?

items.caption: Sam wrote it. Mei wrote his name down.

items.alt: Tuesday, 7:00:05. The Garden Room's display stays on HDMI 1. Priya's laptop: change CHG-3302, 7:00 job disabled, display no change. Sam grins.
items.caption: Tuesday, 07:00:00. The first morning in two years the display stayed where it was left.

items.prompt: Sam writes the problem record's root-cause line. Which one?
items.happening: The fix is verified. The record is what the next person reads.

options.label: “User error: HDMI 2 selected by early users.”
options.result: It's what nine tickets said. It's wrong.
options.fail: The evidence says nobody touched it.

options.label: “Display firmware fault.”
options.fail: The display did exactly what it was told.

options.label: “An orphaned 07:00 job on an unowned legacy scheduler (listed as decommissioned) commanded the display's old address. No owner, so nine incidents never became a problem.”
options.result: Cause, mechanism and the workflow gap, in two sentences, with the evidence linked.
options.consequence: The next person can check every word.

options.label: “Unknown — resolved.”
options.consequence: The tenth ticket arrives next spring.

items.text: 📁 CASE FILE · CASE-016 · SIGNAL original  Ticket Closed  Nine tickets. Nine “Resolved.” One box everyone thought was gone.   Open the case file ▸   Learn · Service · Engineer — it doesn't change your story progress.

items.alt: Sam presents on the meeting-room display: Problem PRB-0231 — nine incidents, one cause, an orphaned 7:00 job with no owner, three more devices affected, change verified Tuesday at 7:00, inventory corrected. Imani listens.

bubbles.text: Nine incidents. One problem. And three other devices nobody knew were being switched every morning.
That's the most important ticket anyone closed this year.

items.alt: Sam at his desk; on his laptop a dialog asks: Delete draft? He's smiling.
items.caption: Two weeks later he became the team's problem manager. The letter stayed deleted.

items.alt: Mei at her desk, holding a printed policy, reading an access request on her screen marked URGENT: tool, vendor remote support; target, the boardroom; requested by R., contractor; reason, the refresh before Monday.

bubbles.text: Remote support. Boardroom. Marked urgent by a contractor called Ray. Who's Ray?

items.caption: Next: *Who Approved This?*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Restore first — but keep the evidence while you do it. Nine identical incidents are one problem nobody owned: link them, give the problem an owner, and look at them on one screen. Catch a scheduled fault at its moment, measured by the network's owner. Inventories record intentions; check them against the world. Finding a cause doesn't make it yours to remove: map what it touches, raise the change, and close the problem only when it's verified at the moment it used to fail.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Sam wasn't bad at his job. He was very good at the only part of it anyone had given him. What part of your work does nobody own?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't prove anything about the room.
